segments.narration: A satellite recorded a nuclear explosion that no country detonated. In September 1979, American satellite Vela 6911 picked up a double flash off the African coast.
Double flashes are the unmistakable signature of an atmospheric nuclear weapon test. The White House convened an emergency panel, while surveillance jets scrambled to sample the air.

While surveillance jets found no airborne particles, low-level fallout was later detected in Australian livestock, and naval hydrophones recorded acoustic signals consistent with an ocean surface blast.
The mystery deepened for decades until declassified documents revealed a hidden partnership. Nuclear intelligence now strongly points to a joint secret test conducted by South Africa and Israel.
Experts suggest the test involved a low-yield nuclear weapon, such as a neutron bomb or artillery round. Did two stealth allies successfully detonate an atomic weapon and hide it from the world?

accuracy_flags.claim: Naval hydrophones detected an acoustic shockwave at the precise millisecond of the flash.
accuracy_flags.note: Sound in water travels much slower than light, so hydrophones could not detect a signal at the exact millisecond of the light flash. Furthermore, the explosion occurred near the ocean surface rather than underground, and low levels of radioactive fallout were detected in Australian sheep.

accuracy_flags.claim: The tested device was a low-yield nuclear warhead designed to minimize radioactive fallout.
accuracy_flags.note: While experts assessed the event as a low-yield nuclear explosion (suggesting a neutron bomb or nuclear artillery round), the reference text does not state that it was intentionally designed to produce minimal fallout to escape global detection.
